lines.text:
The Bakery on the Corner

There is a small bakery on the corner of our street. Every morning, the smell of fresh bread fills the air long before the shop opens at seven.

The baker, Mr Ahmad, starts work at four in the morning. He mixes flour, water, yeast, and salt to make the dough. After kneading it by hand, he lets it rise for about an hour. Then he shapes the dough into loaves, rolls, and baguettes before placing them in the large oven.

By the time the first customers arrive, the shelves are full. There are white bread loaves, wholemeal bread, sourdough, and flatbread. On one side of the counter, there are sweet pastries: croissants, Danish pastries, cinnamon rolls, and doughnuts glazed with sugar. The display case also has cakes — chocolate cake, carrot cake, and cheesecake — all made fresh daily.

Mr Ahmad's wife manages the front of the shop. She serves customers, wraps orders in paper bags, and operates the till. Regular customers often order birthday cakes or wedding cakes in advance.

The bakery also sells biscuits, muffins, and scones with jam and cream. On Fridays, they make a special olive bread that sells out within an hour.

I go there every Saturday to buy a loaf of sourdough and two croissants. The bread is always warm, the crust is golden and crunchy, and the inside is soft. Nothing beats fresh bread from a local bakery.

lines.text: The UK has a strong bread culture: white, wholemeal, granary, tiger bread, and sourdough are all common. Toast with butter is a breakfast staple. 'A sandwich' literally means food between two slices of bread.

lines.text: 'Afternoon tea' is a British tradition: small sandwiches, scones with clotted cream and jam, and cakes served with tea. 'Cream tea' is just scones, cream, and jam. The order — cream first or jam first — is a famous debate!
